comments.author: adrien

On top of this, there is also a relation with the social aspects of open source software: code, documentation and commit messages may be read by someone else and you don't want to look too bad.

You can only have limited amounts of bad code or poor commit messages. You can swear a tiny bit. If you do these too much, you'll look bad, and you get a sense of shame, even if nobody looks at your code.

The last code I wrote took me a bit longer because the shorter way would a) have been a medium-term hindrance I would have to improve anyway, b) have been a forward compatibility issue, c) have looked like corner-cutting, d) have been impossible to explain seriously to others, e) would require more time in explanations and support than code.

comments.author: Kethku
comments.text:
"I find that functionally inarticulate people, almost to a person, also struggle to spell or form grammatically correct sentences on their own because you can't separate the small stuff from the big stuff: when you skimp on getting details correct that bleeds into everything you do and you begin to get the big picture wrong, too."

This reveals a pretty rough bias against people with dyslexia or just people who think differently than you seem to consider correct. Granted I don't think you are necessarily saying the inverse is true (that an inability to spell or form grammatically correct sentences implies that a person is functionally inarticulate) but its an intolerant thing to say either way.

To make a more constructive argument, consider node editors. Node based systems have a lot of problems in their current incarnations but one of the things they can do if built well is filter out classes of syntax errors because they control how the program is authored. Some classes of errors can't be made by construction because the tool won't let you say those things. As an example, if a node takes a string, you can't pass a number. Not because it enforces the constraint at build or heaven forbid runtime, but because you can't say that a number goes there. It only takes strings by construction. Thats a simple example, but other errors such as incorrect loop bounds, wrong argument counts, or some equivalent to parenthesis imbalance could be made impossible to get wrong.

I don't think writing software with a tool that imposes a constraint by construction means you don't understand the constraint. It just means that you don't have to worry about accidentally typing the wrong thing for this class of error. And being frustrated when the tool doesn't take care of the detail of a syntax (like ensuring you have the right number of curly braces in a function to close it out or the right indent level for a part of the logic) doesn't imply that you don't understand why you need to care about the syntax.

I highlight node systems as an example that pulls the llm fire-and-forget-ness/brain off vibe coding out. It isolates the syntax part without the other (in my opinion) more damaging pieces of modern llm usage. Without the llms I think the focus on syntax sorta falls apart a bit.

I agree with the rest of the post. I just think keying on syntax as some underlying indicator of someones ability to understand or write good code is very misguided.

comments.author: Gabriella439
comments.text:
You're correct that I am not necessarily saying the inverse is true.  I'm not claiming that the inability to spell or form grammatically correct sentences implies that a person is functionally inarticulate.

I understand that you're providing this feedback in generosity and good faith, though, and I don't want to come across as defensive. Perhaps there is a way I can adjust the claim so that you don't feel like people with dyslexia are caught in the crossfire.

comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
Previously, on Lobsters, we discussed the phenomenon of folks using System 3 to emit text; by the typical standards of thought, the best explanation for how System 3 utterances are prepared is that the speaker is not thinking. Previously, on Awful, I elaborated how psychology primes us to hope that people are always thinking, either with economic rationality or with some sort of emotional reasoning, despite the evidence showing otherwise. I will readily agree that this is not an issue of essentialism; I don't think that people are fated or doomed or genetically predetermined to rely upon System 3, but that they come to embrace it through interactions with cultural artifacts which spread certain memes.

Regarding two sides of a coin, you might be interested in syntax-semantics duality and the big idea that a programming system is a language (a type theory), a semantics (a bicategory of categories of models), and a pile of functors which sends the language to each of its semantics. From this perspective, there can be a distinction between concrete and abstract syntax.

comments.author: hwayne
comments.text:
To illustrate what I mean, I recently audited an LLM prompt and stumbled across this:


Never suggest external tools or alternatives that aren't part of the skills listed above. If a task requires capabilities beyond the available skills, say so.


This is the sort of prompt that I would read as functionally inarticulate: it sounds sensible if you don't read closely but when you do you might notice the prompt is actually giving the model two diametrically opposed instructions.


At the risk of proving myself functionally inarticulate, how are these opposed? Saying "I can't do this with the skills you provided" is consistent with both instructions. If the last sentence was "if the task requires ... skills, say which ones you need" then they'd be opposed, but as it stands I don't see the inconsistency.

comments.author: paulocuambe
comments.text:
I really like this advice.
When I’m learning a new programming language my preferred way of doing it is in a text editor without syntax highlighting and code completion. I type the program, try to compile it, see the error message, fix and iterate.

As an any person, I’m usually biased by previous programming experiences, so sometimes I make assumptions and find out they work or they don’t while compiling.

I actually do all my programming this way and I keep learning new things. I usually don’t have to look up the documentation a lot after some time with the language. I know the std libraries of the languages I pretty well.

I should also mention that I read through the standard library documentation [and code] of the PLs to fine-tune my intuition.

Side note: I really enjoy programming. I enjoy reading and understanding things about computers. I like giving precise instructions to the machine and see it achieve the goal I set. I do not understand why people offload such joyful activity to AIs. The best decision in my life was to study computer science. Computers are such amazing and complex creatures. Dedicating a lifetime to learning about them is something I really look forward to and have enjoyed so far.

I have this overall feeling that when I have a clear concept of what I'm doing, the syntax+structure just flows. In fact, it's a signal I've learned to connect with. If I'm struggling with the syntax then it's rarely a skill issue - it's my mental model is incomplete.

comments.author: deemas
comments.text:
Cognitive science doesn't really support "learning styles" pop theory. Same with "multiple intelligences". Psychometry papers largely recognize a single factor "g" that correlates strongly with every measure of cognitive performance.

It's not unlike physical exercise. There are no different ways to gain strength, no different "styles" of improving athletic performance. You just need to do a lot of what the performance is.

Knowledge work is processing symbols. You need to process a lot of symbols. The most straightforward way to do that is read a lot, write a lot, and verify correctness often. That's what gets me the most about using LLMs. Seeking to write and read very little and deferring verification to an unreliable tool cannot possible yield gains to any cognitive system, be it individual or collective.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
I agree there’s no real evidence for fixed "learning styles" in the pop-psych sense.

But that's different from saying modality or approach never matters (which is the point I wanted to make, even if that didn't land).

The most effective medium often depends a lot on context and preferences. Diagrams can be excellent for architecture and systems thinking. Hands-on work is usually better for implementation fluency. Worked examples can help early understanding before deliberate practice takes over.

"Knowledge work is processing symbols" feels true only if you define symbols so broadly that it includes diagrams, spatial models, interfaces, and direct manipulation -- that's overly broad to be practical and I think is too tautological.

Improvement comes from doing the thing, which I broadly agree with. But that still doesn’t imply there's a single effective mode of getting there.

comments.author: deemas
comments.text:
Fair enough but the points being argued are "syntax is abstract thought", "but some people might struggle with syntax even if they don't with abstract thought" and "that means they should do more syntax not that they are inherently tuned towards some types of abstract thought but not others" which I think is a solid chain and I don't think you've shown the final conclusion to be invalid.

Knowledge work is processing symbols is not something I came up with, I'm following on the footsteps of Christopher Alexander's "Notes on the Synthesis of Form" and Herbert Simon's "The Science of The Artificial" and leaning heavily on the equivalence of symbolic computation and formal logic to rely on the universality of my claim. It might be tautological but mathematics often is, the corollary of a given set of assumptions is not always obvious from their formulation alone and some 'tautological' (that is, logically sound) expansion is needed.

comments.author: Gabriella439
comments.text:
The reason the post ignores the economy of learning is because that's not the goal of the post.  If I were to unpack every counterargument that one might raise then the post would be incoherent and unfocused.  I usually try to write posts that explain one thing and explain it well and then subsequent posts can build upon ideas introduced in previous posts.

However, I do believe it is worth putting in the effort.  There's actually a whole section from the post I cut out while editing which included this anecdote:


I've reviewed many agentically-coded pull requests and given feedback asking for small cleanups like "could you factor out this duplicate code into a shared function" or "could you split this out into a separate module".  Most would oblige, unsurprisingly, because they have an agent to do this drudgery for them; I heartily approve!

However, a couple of these agentic coders would consistently push back against the cleanup requests.  They wouldn't object to these requests on the merits; rather, they would portray the small refactor as an extraordinary imposition.  This initially caught me by surprise since I thought they could just forward the request to their agent, but eventually I began to learn that no amount of technology can save a person who loses faith in their own self-efficacy


Coding with a model might work for a bit, but as your own skills atrophy and you lose confidence in your ability to do the task or even review the model's output the more you will become unable to properly drive the model and then you end up helpless like the latter group of agentic coders.  That's where the economics of agentic coding fare poorly.

comments.author: tentacloids
comments.text:
You should be learning on the job because that increases your knowledge, value, and ultimately agency as a labourer in the future. If your job prevented you from seeing your family before LLMs because of your typing speed, you were being exploited; now you are choosing to provide work without getting as much as you should in return. Great..?

I hope you appreciate the irony in defending the use of one of the pointy parts of capitalism in order to combat another. LLMs aren't the only tool you can use to control your own work-life balance, and I'm pretty sure they're not the most effective (and so defending them specifically seems a bit odd). It's not as if employers don't know about them either, so they are surely a short-term band-aid.

Advocate for yourself, not the machine!
